t65z11_fg1p2w1p1: What can help is seeing what shaped the harm they did. Their conditioning and history went into it. So did their pain, and what they could and couldn't do. Hurt people often pass on pain they never worked through. With everything they'd become by then, it was their only move. You might hear that as a moral instruction, like now you're supposed to understand them. When you see it for yourself, though, forgiveness may come on its own. And your rage at them as the only one to blame can soften into something more accurate.
t65z11_fg1p4w1p1: Forgiving yourself works the same way. Own what you did, and only what was yours. Let the remorse in, that "I wish I hadn't" feeling. Repair what you can by apologizing and making amends. Changing how you act counts too. Then you're allowed to stop holding yourself hostage. That can feel like getting away with something. The responsibility stays, though. When forgiving yourself is hard, forgiving other people tends to be harder too. Some harms take years. Forgiving too soon is one trap, and the other is staying resentful for good. Don't push it. Come back over time to the question of how they became capable of what they did, until the understanding is real enough that you feel differently.

The responsibility stays, though. With other people, some harms take years to forgive. Forgiving too soon is one trap, and living permanently inside resentment is the other. Don't push it. Over time, keep coming back to how they became capable of what they did, until the understanding is real enough to change how you feel.
t65z11_le1p2w1p1: Ask yourself what has really ended, and what you're still trying to keep going. What isn't known yet? And what is your little one afraid will happen in the gap? It might not have the words yet. What practical act or small ritual would mark the ending without pretending you know the next beginning? Don't force a new you just because not knowing feels unbearable. The grown-up you can keep your routines and protect your body. Grieving what ended is part of it, and so is staying with your little one while the next life takes shape.

A meal or a boundary can help, and so can a kind sentence, but they don't touch the question underneath: "Why should I want this life at all?" Maybe you've caught yourself asking it. t65z11_fg1p1w1p1: For many people, healing eventually includes some forgiveness, or at least getting out from under active resentment. You can't schedule it. And you don't need it first to be safe (please don't wait) or set boundaries. Holding someone accountable and getting justice can come first, and recovering can too. While you're actively resenting them, your view can narrow. Your little one can stay built around the injury, too. Maybe you feel you should be over it by now. But forgiving early under pressure gets you an enlightened-looking performance while the wound goes underground.
t65z11_le1p3w2p1: Missing someone doesn't have to be another problem to solve. Don't push the missing away. Sometimes the ache itself can become a cue for love. Maybe you're already saying "I miss you" in your head. If love is there, let that turn into "I love you," or offer a simple wish: "May you be safe. May you be held in love." Picture them, or just feel the care going out to them. You don't have to believe they receive anything, since this is about what happens in you. It doesn't replace grieving or being in touch with them. You'd still keep whatever boundaries you need, and do the practical things. If sending love makes you more compulsive or unreal, make it simpler: "I miss you, and I care." Do the same if you can't get back to your life. You can also offer some of that care to the part of you that's still here.

## How Much Happiness Do You Know Is Possible?

Part of love is wanting someone to be well, and how far that wish can reach depends partly on what kind of happiness you know is possible. If the happiness you know is food, safety, affection, friends, work that means something and some help when you need it, then wanting those things for somebody is love. Babies get some of this already. Practical love matters a lot.

But a big spiritual experience can show you a kind of peace, or a love, you didn't know existed, and then "I want you to be happy" suddenly means something much bigger. That's partly why loving-kindness meditation can sound almost comically simple to someone who's never been near what it's pointing at, and so powerful to someone who has. Saying "may you be happy" over and over isn't automatically some profound love. It's one way of finding that deeper love and growing it.

If you're curious about that bigger happiness, follow the curiosity instead of pretending to believe something. Read people from different traditions, and meet people whose lives make you wonder. You might already know someone like that, who's happy in a way you can't quite figure out. And judge a path by its fruits: what are the people who follow it like?

Sometimes your whole life, as far ahead as you can see, feels too small. Care isn't what's missing then. A meal or a boundary can help, and so can a kind sentence, but they don't touch the question underneath: "Why should I want this life at all?" Maybe you've caught yourself asking it. Take that question seriously. Right now being alive might feel like something to get through. What would have to be possible for it to feel worth discovering?

Curiosity can be enough here, something like "Other people say they've felt a depth of love or peace that I never have. I don't know if I believe their explanation. But what if the experience is possible for me?" Don't assume the limits of what you've felt so far are the limits of what's possible.

# Borrowed Adulthood in Relationship

Reparenting is usually talked about as something you do alone, or with a therapist. But your little one got hurt in relationships, and that kind of hurt can only heal so far on your own. Sometimes one person ends up doing a lot of the borrowed grown-up jobs at once. They cook, they keep track of the appointments, they drive, they're the one who says it'll be okay, or they're just the competent person in the room. Maybe you're picturing them right now. Having someone like that while you're struggling can be an enormous blessing.

Over time, reparenting can help you take in and practice some of what that person has shown you. Maybe you've already caught yourself saying "it'll be okay" the way they do. Other jobs can be shared with friends and community. Professionals or services can help, and so can routines and simple tools. The aim is for your little one to feel reliably cared for from more than one place, while the relationship itself stays precious and important. Which of those jobs can become more yours, and which are healthiest shared? And which really belong inside that relationship?
